subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the relative charge of a proton?
questions.explain: A proton carries a relative charge of +1, equal and opposite to that of an electron.

questions.q: The mass number of an atom is the total number of which particles?
options: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus
questions.explain: The mass number equals the number of protons plus the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.q: Isotopes of the same element have which of the following?
options: The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
Different numbers of protons and neutrons
The same number of protons and neutrons
questions.explain: Isotopes share the same proton (atomic) number but differ in their number of neutrons.

questions.q: An atom has a mass number of 23 and an atomic number of 11. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.q: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of which particle?
questions.explain: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons so the charges cancel.

questions.q: An alpha particle is identical to which of the following?
options: A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons)
questions.explain: An alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, making it a helium nucleus.

questions.q: What is a beta particle?
questions.explain: A beta particle is a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus during beta decay.

questions.q: Gamma radiation is best stopped by which of the following?
options: A thick sheet of lead or concrete
Nothing can reduce it at all
questions.explain: Gamma is the most penetrating radiation and needs thick lead or concrete to reduce it significantly.

questions.q: What is the unit used to measure the activity of a radioactive source?
questions.explain: Activity is measured in becquerels, where one becquerel is one decay per second.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are the most ionising because of their large charge and mass, though they are least penetrating.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, how do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2
Mass number decreases by 2 and atomic number decreases by 4
Mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1
questions.explain: Losing 2 protons and 2 neutrons reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.q: During beta decay a neutron changes into a proton. What happens to the nucleus?
options: The atomic number increases by 1 and the mass number stays the same
The atomic number decreases by 1 and the mass number stays the same
The mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2
Both the mass number and atomic number increase by 1
questions.explain: Gaining a proton raises the atomic number by 1, while the total number of nucleons is unchanged.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is best described as which of the following?
options: The time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
The time taken for all the nuclei in a sample to decay
The time taken for the activity of a sample to double
Half of the total time a sample takes to decay completely
questions.explain: Half-life is the average time for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, halving the activity.

questions.q: A radioactive sample has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. What is its activity after 6 hours?
questions.explain: Six hours is three half-lives, so the activity halves three times: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 Bq.

questions.q: After four half-lives, what fraction of the original radioactive nuclei remains undecayed?
questions.explain: The fraction remaining is (1/2) to the power 4, which equals 1/16.

questions.q: Which isotope is commonly used as the fuel in nuclear fission reactors?
questions.explain: Uranium-235 is a fissile isotope that undergoes fission when it absorbs a neutron.

questions.q: What is the purpose of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and control the rate of fission
To release extra neutrons into the core
questions.explain: Control rods absorb neutrons, reducing the number available to cause further fissions and controlling the reaction.

questions.q: Nuclear fission is the process in which which of the following occurs?
options: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
Two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus
An electron is emitted from the nucleus
A nucleus emits a helium nucleus
questions.explain: In fission a large unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and further neutrons.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun, involves which of the following?
options: Two small nuclei joining to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy
A large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
A nucleus absorbing a neutron and becoming unstable
A nucleus emitting a beta particle
questions.explain: Fusion joins light nuclei, such as hydrogen isotopes, into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy as in the Sun.

questions.q: Fusion in the Sun requires extremely high temperatures. Why is this needed?
options: The nuclei need enough energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them
High temperatures are needed to split the nuclei apart
The neutrons must be slowed down before they can fuse
High temperature is needed to absorb the emitted electrons
questions.explain: Positively charged nuclei repel each other, so very high temperatures give them enough kinetic energy to collide and fuse.
